paragraphs.text: Hey, Adam. Welcome to the show. Thanks for having me. Before we get started, why don't you give everybody a bit about your background? Health. And the health actually started very shortly after employee benefits, which was the pension. And then we had a record keeper. We actually sold that to Empower this year.

And the fourth is property and casualty. So health emerged in the 50s and then life shortly thereafter. And so our practice in financial risk management was born out of the Chicago mergers and acquisitions practice that helped life insurers with M&A and other traditional life consulting. So we then helped them understand how to hedge that like a bank would. And then we initially it was consulting and software. No standing next to our desk because we're trying to innovate some of the more complex derivatives from Lehman Brothers to other banks that the insurers were holding. Right. So that's how we developed a pension for risk management inside of mutual funds. And then that led us to the ETF industry. So these are ETFs, Milliman's first ETFs. And so just out of curiosity, before we talk about the two of them, why ETFs and why start in health care? So. We as we were looking at this problem and we started looking at this problem with our colleagues in health. A little over three and a half years ago. And we found that this is really kind of endemic to both institutions and individuals.

The rising cost of care is affecting everybody. So not only those that are trying to insure it, but those are trying to save for it. So we work for most of the large organizations in the health care system. And I would say the most overall. So we actually put out two indices that measure this differently for individuals. So the first one I'll cite is the Milliman Retiree Healthcare Cost Index. That measures how much money a individual or a couple will spend over their retirement lifespan.

So once they retire to when they pass. And the total spend over that period for a male with the original Medicare plus Medigap, which is Plan G, plus the Medicare Part D, the drugs, is $297,000 for a male and $340,000 for a female. So over $600,000 for a couple in retirement. And that's up on the order of 7% from last year's study and certainly rising over time.

And that's with Medicare, right? I think that's what a lot of people don't understand is even if you have that backstop, you still have to have money saved in order to pay for a really basic plan. So that's in retirement. The next one is that we put out is called the Milliman Medical Index. And the Milliman Medical Index measures the cost of providing either an individual just on a corporate healthcare plan. So all of your deductibles out of pocket, everything like that. And then also a typical family of four. So that number for this year was $37,000 for a family of four is how much one needs just in a corporate health plan and $8,460 for an average person.

So the rate of inflation in that number that we've been measuring since 2005 is over 6% per year. So well above someone's typical raise if they're trying to fund this just out of their salary. So the ETFs, so how do we try to address this problem with an investment strategy? So obviously that rate of inflation is well more than tips, is well more than treasuries, right? You have to end up taking some risk in order to get to higher returns. So the way that we do that is there's a third index we publish.

And the third index tracks claims inflation. So we actually look at claims that are, we buy data and we get data from providers. So from health plans, and then we track how much the claims are increasing over time. And we call that, healthcare actuaries call that trend. So the trend in those claims kind of matches what we see in the medical, minimum medical index. So anywhere from 5% to 6%. It's lately been running well over that. It's almost 7% in the last five years or so. So the health trend guidelines index, that's what that index is.

We use that as our bogey for the strategy, okay? So the strategy then seeks to meet that rate of return to try to match that bogey over time by investing in healthcare equities. But in healthcare equities in a specific way where we identify, I like to call it a follow the money strategy. We try to identify the companies that benefit when certain trends in inflation are high in healthcare, right? So right now, the trends are high because of drugs. So we're identifying the companies that are benefiting from the drug costs.

And the biggest one right now is Lilly, for example. And that's our biggest holding in the healthcare space. So that's healthcare equities. There's also a layer that we call a supply chain, which is broad equities. So that's all the other things that could cause inflation in a lot of things. So technology gets more expensive or other things kind of in the broader economy get more expensive. That also pushes up healthcare inflation. Then we have diversifier bucket. And the diversifier that we've chosen serves really two purposes. So one is to reduce the equity exposure in a drawdown. So we want something that tends to not be correlated to equities in a drawdown and has potential to appreciate.

And that's gold. But then we also like gold because when paired with our treasury, which is our de-risking bucket, gold plus treasuries tends to keep up with wage inflation over time. And then our final bucket is a treasury strategy in particular that we dial in in order to try to match wage inflation. So that's how we kind of construct the portfolio to build up to how we seek to meet that level of healthcare inflation. And that's the guard strategy I just described. And then for plus, the plus aims 2% above that health trend every single month.

And we rebalance that approach. Some things on a weekly basis, everything else on a monthly basis when we get the new reading from our healthcare actuaries. So plus, it shoots 2% above the bogey by taking more risk necessarily in equities, but in the same general way to try to outpace inflation over time. Okay. So let me try to simplify this for the advisors and the listeners. So MHIG is the bogey, right? You're going to try to match the cost of inflation in the healthcare sector. The MHIP is the bogey plus two.

And you're going to do that by taking more risk. So very interested in how you're putting this strategy together in order to do that. Because your team has a ton of experience. You guys have spent years on volatility and risk management and 40-act portfolios. But you're kind of taking this portfolio mix from what I'm hearing in healthcare equities, broad equities, treasuries, tips, corporates, gold now, and commodities. So every single month, we have a projected that we get from our actuaries, a projection on what the trend is right now.

Now, that is based on what has happened roughly five months ago. So when you submit your claim to your doctor, it takes a while for it to get resolved and fully paid. Sometimes there's a back and forth between the insurer and the provider. So all of that stuff resolves roughly five months later. So we get essentially what's like a now cast of that healthcare inflation. What is it likely trending at right now? Given that, and then given our model's expected return assumptions for those asset classes, we assemble the portfolio with the least amount of risk possible in order to meet that objective over that month.

And then we do the same thing month over month over month. And then we also have other features in the equity side that try to help control volatility and drawdown per specific security. So we're trying to identify the securities that are experiencing, maybe some device manufacturer has a recall and it's, that stock is experiencing a drawdown. So our systems are constantly monitoring all that and pulling away from that stock and putting into something else that may not have so much of an issue that's more correlated with the inflation that we're seeing over time.

So basically, we're taking as much risk as we need to, but not more to seek our objective. So it seems to be like your edge here is the fact that you, the, the closeness to the data and the history in which you guys have, have been doing this, which, gives you that edge. Just curious, is that monthly rebalance like a fully rules-based approach? And then those, we'll call them, additional drawdown protection. Is that inter-month or is that, is that also rules-based or there, you have analysts on this, like just kind of curious of the construction and I guess monitoring, a continuous monitoring of the product.

Yeah. So it's all data-driven. So we don't have a analysts that are, that are going through all this data because it is so significant. But what we've built into our strategy is the ideas that our health colleagues have had over time, right? So we, we are, we are using some AI in this to help understand when a particular company is having a problem, right? And, may need to be kind of backed away from due to some regulatory activity. So we're monitoring information from the CMS, from the FDA, from state regulators, even legal filings and, and things like that in order to understand the idiosyncratic risk in each of the individual companies.

And then we're also using the claims data to understand the drivers of inflation right now. So for example, right now we're seeing pharma trends are really high, but then hospital and professional services are, are kind of flat. The, um, the, the risk management, uh, with, kind of the, the, um, those sentiment factors from regulators that I described and, and then other factors is done on a weekly basis.
